uni-hotel-ops.title: Hotel Management: Front Office, F&B, Housekeeping & Kitchen
uni-hotel-ops.description: A hands-on study companion for hotel-management students and new hospitality staff: front office, food & beverage service, housekeeping and kitchen operations with worked numericals and real guest scenarios. Independent study material; it does not replace supervised training.

courses.title: Front Office Operations
courses.summary: Reservations, check-in to check-out, room-status control, key performance numbers (occupancy, ADR, RevPAR), night audit and handling guest complaints.
outcomes: Learners can run the guest cycle from reservation to departure
Learners can compute occupancy, ADR and RevPAR
Learners can handle an overbooking and a complaint using a recovery framework
Learners can explain what a night audit does

lessons.title: Lab: Overbooked on a conference weekend

scenes.text: It is 6 pm on a conference weekend. Ankit, the front desk agent, finds that a guest with a guaranteed booking has arrived but every room is taken.
The guest has travelled all day and is tired. The manager on duty is in a meeting.

steps.title: Why hotels overbook
steps.body: Some guests cancel or do not show up. Hotels sell slightly more rooms than they have, using past no-show data. Occasionally everyone arrives and the hotel must **walk** a guest: arrange a comparable room elsewhere at the hotel's cost.

steps.title: A recovery framework
steps.body:
- Apologise sincerely and take ownership
- Offer a comparable hotel, transport and a phone call or message home
- Offer the guest a room back on the next night
- Escalate to the duty manager and record the incident

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Blaming the system or the reservations team
- Walking a guest without telling them where they are going
- Forgetting to log the incident

lessons.title: Lab: Compute occupancy, ADR and RevPAR

scenes.text: The general manager asks the front-office manager for yesterday's numbers before the 9 am meeting.
The hotel has 120 rooms; 90 were sold and room revenue was ₹6,30,000.

steps.title: The three numbers
steps.body:
- **Occupancy %** = rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100
- **ADR** (average daily rate) = room revenue ÷ rooms sold
- **RevPAR** (revenue per available room) = room revenue ÷ rooms available = occupancy × ADR

steps.title: Why RevPAR matters
steps.body: High occupancy with deep discounts can still give poor RevPAR. Managers look at all three together.

scenes.text: Meera books online, arrives, stays two nights and leaves. Every stage has a front-office task behind it.
Missing one stage, such as taking an imprint or card pre-authorisation, can cost the hotel money.

steps.title: Four stages
steps.body:
- **Pre-arrival:** reservation, confirmation, special requests.
- **Arrival:** registration, ID check (Form C for foreign nationals in India), room assignment, key.
- **Occupancy:** posting charges, handling requests, information.
- **Departure:** bill settlement, key return, feedback, folio closing.

steps.title: Room status
steps.body: Common codes: vacant clean, vacant dirty, occupied, on-change, out of order. Housekeeping and front office must agree on these every day.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving a room before housekeeping releases it.
- Posting a charge to the wrong room folio.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – the night auditor's decisions

scenes.text: Rahul, the night auditor, closes the day: verifies postings, reconciles cash and updates statistics.
He finds that room 305 was charged ₹2,400 for a minibar item the guest says he never used.

steps.title: What a night audit does
steps.body: The night audit verifies that every charge was posted to the right folio, balances the day's cash and card totals, posts room and tax charges, produces the manager's report and rolls the date forward.

steps.title: Error handling
steps.body: Never delete a posting. Post a correcting adjustment with a reason code and get supervisor approval; the audit trail must stay intact.

steps.title: Escalate
steps.body: Anything above your approval limit or involving suspected fraud goes to the duty manager in writing.

lessons.title: Lab: Order the steps of table service

scenes.text: Karan joins a restaurant as a trainee waiter. His captain says service is a sequence; skipping a step shows.
A family of four is seated at table 7.

steps.title: Service styles
steps.body:
- **Plated (American):** food is plated in the kitchen.
- **Silver (French/English):** served from platters at the table.
- **Buffet:** guests help themselves.
- **Gueridon:** finishing or carving on a trolley beside the table.

steps.title: Sequence
steps.body: Greet and seat, water and menus, take beverage order, serve beverages, take food order, serve in order (ladies/guests of honour first by tradition), check back, clear, dessert, bill, farewell.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Serving from the wrong side.
- Clearing while others still eat.
- Not repeating the order back.

lessons.title: Lab: Cost a dish and price the menu

scenes.text: Chef wants to add a paneer starter. The manager wants food cost near 30%.
Total ingredient cost per portion is ₹90.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Food cost %** = food cost ÷ food sales × 100
- **Selling price** = cost ÷ target cost %
- **Average spend per cover** = revenue ÷ covers

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Cost ₹90, target 30%: price = 90 ÷ 0.30 = **₹300** (before tax).
Month: cost ₹36,000 on sales ₹1,20,000 gives 36000 ÷ 120000 = **30%**.
200 covers earning ₹84,000 gives **₹420** per cover.

steps.title: Round sensibly
steps.body: Round to a menu-friendly price (₹299 or ₹305) and recheck the cost %.

steps.title: Par stock
steps.body: A **par** is the number of sets needed to keep one set in each place: in use, in the laundry, in storage/floor cupboards, and sometimes a reserve. Par 4 means 4 sets per bed.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: 60 rooms × 2 beds = 120 beds. At par 4: 120 × 4 = **480** sheet sets.

steps.title: Temperature control
steps.body: Bacteria multiply fastest in the **danger zone**, roughly between 5°C and 60°C. Keep cold food at or below 5°C and hot food above 60°C, cool cooked food quickly, reheat thoroughly, and separate raw from ready-to-eat items to avoid cross-contamination.
